digo: Chivumbani cha chigala; Mnyururika; Mtsusa tsalu
digo_source: Pakia (2005) App. III, App. V, App. VI

teaser.en: Its leaves turn slippery when crushed, and they were used to polish beads clean.

summary.en: *Chivumbani cha chigala* is a weedy herb with yellow flowers and burr fruits that stick to clothes. Its other names describe how its crushed leaves turn slippery and are used to clean beads.

about.en: *Triumfetta rhomboidea* is an upright herb or small sub-shrub with hairy stems and roughly diamond-shaped, toothed leaves. Its small yellow flowers grow in clusters along the stems. The small round fruits are covered in hooked bristles and catch on fur and clothing. Digo identify it by its leaves.

where.en: It is a common weed of farmland, roadsides, fallow and disturbed ground throughout the tropics.

uses.en: Pakia records that the leaves are crushed and used as a medicine; when crushed they give a slippery extract. The leaves are also used to clean beads, which gives the name *mtsusa tsalu*.

names.en: The plant has three Digo names. *Mnyururika* means 'slippery extract', from *nyururika*, to be slippery. *Mtsusa tsalu* means 'bead cleaner', from *tsusa*, to clean, and *tsalu*, beads. Pakia gives it as an example of a name describing a general use. Both names are shared with *Waltheria indica*, and *mtsusa tsalu* also with *Abutilon zanzibaricum*. Pakia gives no meaning for *chivumbani cha chigala*. Its first word is the Digo name of tree basil, *chivumbani* (*Ocimum suave*).

reason.en: Waltheria indica, which shares two names
Abutilon zanzibaricum, also called mtsusa tsalu
Tree basil, whose name it borrows
